claims.text: Chemical short-range order suppresses lattice thermal conductivity in concentrated refractory high-entropy alloys relative to a fully random solid solution.
SRO-induced local strain fields enhance phonon scattering.
Heterogeneous local bond stiffening reduces phonon group velocities.
High-temperature homogenization followed by rapid quenching can produce a nearly random solid solution with negligible SRO.
Moderate-temperature annealing below the solvus and above the diffusion activation threshold can induce SRO without producing long-range order or phase separation.
Annealing between 0.4 and 0.6 times the melting temperature is an appropriate regime for establishing steady-state SRO.
Rapid quenching after annealing preserves the annealing-induced SRO state at room temperature.
Non-random atomic distributions generate local lattice distortions and fluctuating force constants.
The spatially varying potential associated with SRO scatters mid-to-long-wavelength phonons more effectively than the corresponding random-alloy configuration.
SRO can reduce local mass-variance fluctuations relative to a random atomic distribution.
In refractory alloys, correlated strain fields and bond-stiffness variations dominate over the reduction in mass-fluctuation scattering.
SRO correlations act as resonant or strong phonon-scattering centers.
Phonons whose wavelengths are comparable to the SRO correlation length are especially strongly scattered.
The enhanced scattering associated with SRO reduces phonon mean free path and lattice thermal conductivity.
The SRO-containing alloy will have lower lattice thermal conductivity than the random alloy from 300 K to 1000 K.
The conductivity suppression will be strongest between 300 K and 600 K because phonon-phonon scattering is less dominant there than point-defect and structural scattering.
The proposed suppression requires sufficiently large atomic-size mismatch and elastic-modulus differences to generate strong local strain fields upon ordering.
The hypothesis may not apply when SRO develops into a long-range-ordered superlattice or is too weak to appreciably change the phonon-scattering cross-section.
An SRO sample with statistically significant Warren-Cowley parameters but conductivity equal to or greater than the random control between 300 K and 600 K would falsify the hypothesis.
A longer phonon mean free path in the SRO sample than in the random sample would favor a reduced-scattering or ordering-dominated regime and reject the proposed scattering-dominated mechanism.
